newsitem.title: USA: CellPro patent dispute with Baxter/Becton resumes.
newsitem.headline: CellPro patent dispute with Baxter/Becton resumes.

text.p: CellPro Inc's patent dispute with Johns Hopkins University, Baxter Healthcare Corp and Becton Dickinson and Co was back in court Tuesday with a new jury trial.
In August 1995, a federal jury found that four Johns Hopkins patents for an anti-body used in bone marrow transplants were invalid and that CellPro products did not infringe them.

But after the trial Judge Roderick McKelvie, of the U.S. District Court in Delaware, effectively reversed the jury's decision by ruling in favor of Johns Hopkins and its licensee, Becton Dickinson, on a series of motions challenging the characterization of the patent claims in the jury trial and CellPro's defenses against them.

This new jury must decide two issues based on only two of the four original patents: what damages should be awarded to plaintiffs Johns Hopkins, Becton Dickinson and Baxter, and whether or not those damages should be increased up to three times for alleged willful infringement.
Baxter is a party because it bought an exclusive license from Becton Dickinson for 5.5 percent of patent-related product sales.

In opening arguments Tuesday, plaintiff attorney Donald Ware asked the jury to award damages of about $1.6 million based on a royalty of eight percent charged against CellPro's $17 million in alleged infringing sales plus a percentage of an up-front fee of $750,000.

Cellpro attorney Coe Bloomberg asked that the royalty be no more than four percent, or $680,000. He also asserted that Cellpro was "reasonable" and not willful when it acted on a legal opinion that the Johns Hopkins patents were invalid.
Bloomberg restated CellPro's claim the patents were invalid because they had been anticipated by earlier inventions.
He said that, in December, Cellpro's CEPRATE SC System became the first and only cell processing system to receive marketing approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
CellPro chief executive Richard Murdock, in Delaware to observe the five to six day trial, told Reuters: "The damages are not going to have any significant financial impact on us.
"We're looking ahead to the appeals...We've tried to negotiate (with Baxter and Becton Dickinson), but they don't want to talk now. They want to get a judgement against us if they can."
Murdock said a CellPro antitrust lawsuit against the plaintiffs has been stayed pending the outcome of the damages trial.
CellPro, of Bothell, Washington, is a biotechnology company that sells continuous-flow cell-selection systems for therapeutic, diagnostic and research applications.
Becton Dickinson is a Franklin Lakes, New Jersey manufacturer of medical devices and diagnostic products.
Baxter is a Deerfield, Illinois manufacturer of health care products.F
